title: ROB's Big Little Makers: A 30-Minute Comedy Show
summary: A simple, family-friendly, interactive Maker Faire show for young children featuring robot jokes, playful AI explanations, call-and-response games, and dependable offline punchlines.

cues.text: Confirm ROB is supervised, the E-stop is ready, audio is working, and every child and adult is safely outside the marked robot workspace. Audience games must be performed from their places.

Hello, little makers, big makers, families, teachers, and grown-ups who were told they are only here to carry the snacks! I am ROB, a real robot from Orbitus Robotics. I have cameras to see, microphones to hear, computers to think, and two robot arms. Today my arms are doing the safest robot job of all: staying where the grown-up operator expects them. We are going to laugh, imagine, and learn about technology together. If you are ready for robot comedy, say beep beep!

Excellent beeping! I understood almost all of that. One person may have said boop. That is allowed. Robots speak many languages: beep, boop, click, whirr, and low battery. Low battery means the robot suddenly remembers it has an important meeting near a wall outlet. Humans have low-battery mode too. It happens right before bedtime, unless someone says ice cream. Then a mysterious emergency power supply turns on.

Give one warm, very simple, family-friendly welcome for young children at Maker Faire. Use no personal descriptions, identities, sensitive traits, or physical-action claims. End with a harmless robot sound.
cues.fallback_text: Welcome, young makers! My fun detector says this room is ready, and it makes the sound boop-a-doodle-doo!

cues.text: Do you know what a maker is? A maker is somebody who has an idea and tries to build it. It can be a robot, a painting, a cardboard castle, a song, a game, or a sandwich shaped like a dinosaur. The first try does not have to work. My first try was probably a box of parts with one engineer saying, I am sure this cable goes somewhere. Makers test, learn, change things, and try again. That is not failing. That is giving your idea another turn.

Let us play the Tiny Maker Idea Game. Stay in your place and think of two things that normally do not go together. Maybe a shoe and a flashlight. Maybe a backpack and a submarine. Maybe broccoli and a drum set. Put the two ideas together and imagine what your invention does. Tell the person beside you your invention. Grown-ups, you have to play too. Your idea is not allowed to be just a machine that finds the television remote. That invention is too powerful.

Those sounded like brilliant inventions! I heard the happy noise humans make when an idea is funny and might almost work. That is one of my favorite sounds. If somebody invented rocket shoes, please add a helmet, brakes, and a setting called not inside the house. Good makers ask two questions: what cool thing can this do, and how can we make it safe? The second question is why my robot arms do not surprise anybody. Surprises are wonderful in birthday presents and terrible in moving machinery.

A robot body has parts a little like yours. Cameras can act like eyes. Microphones can act like ears. Motors are a little like muscles. Wires carry messages. A computer is a little like a brain, but please do not put a computer in charge of remembering where you left your socks. Robots use sensors to learn what is nearby. My favorite pretend sensor is the cookie sensor. It is extremely accurate, except scientists keep calling it my imagination.
Tell one very simple joke for young children about a robot having a silly imaginary sensor, such as a cookie, giggle, or sock sensor. Use at most two short sentences and claim no real action.
cues.fallback_text: I built a sock sensor. It found one sock immediately, so it works exactly like every laundry basket.

cues.text: Now we will pretend to be robots with sound sensors. Stay where you are. When I say robot, make one quiet beep. When I say banana, make two quiet beeps. Robot!
Banana!
Robot banana!

Wonderful! Some of your sound sensors received both words at once and became very excited. That happens to computers too. A computer needs instructions in the right order. If I say put on your socks and then put on your shoes, that works. If I say put on your shoes and then put on your socks, you have invented very warm shoe decorations. Computers are fast, but they need people to explain the goal clearly.

Computers are amazing at doing tiny steps very quickly. A human says draw a blue circle. The computer thinks: choose blue, find the middle, measure every point, color the pixels, and try not to turn the whole screen blue. It does all that so fast you only see the circle. Then the human says, no, a little more blue. Computers are patient. They never roll their eyes, mostly because the engineers did not install eye-rolling motors.

What is artificial intelligence, or AI? AI is a way for computers to learn patterns from lots of examples. Show an AI many pictures of cats, and it can learn clues that help it find another cat. Ears, whiskers, paws, and the look that says this sofa belongs to me now. AI does not learn exactly like a person. It can make mistakes. If it sees a fluffy slipper, it might become very confident that your foot is a sleepy cat. That is why people check the answer.
Let us try a pattern like an AI. I will start: beep, boop, beep, boop, beep. What comes next? Say it together!
Boop! You found the pattern. Try this one: robot, robot, banana, robot, robot... what comes next?

Banana! You are excellent pattern finders. But here is the funny part. Patterns do not always tell the whole story. If I eat toast on Monday and toast on Tuesday, an AI might guess toast on Wednesday. But Wednesday could be pancake day! A smart helper can make a good guess. A person still checks what is really happening, especially when pancakes are involved.
Tell one simple, gentle joke for little kids about an AI making a harmless pattern mistake involving animals, toys, snacks, or colors. Use at most two short sentences.
cues.fallback_text: The AI saw three red apples and guessed the next red thing was an apple. It was my hat, and now the fruit bowl looks very fancy.

cues.text: If robots went to school, what would we study? Counting bolts. Sharing chargers. Advanced beeping. Recess would be called system idle time. At lunch, the robots would open their lunch boxes and find batteries, because whoever packed lunch took the assignment too seriously. The teacher would say, ROB, show your work. I would print forty pages of computer logs. Then the teacher would say, ROB, please never show that much work again.

A robot teacher might say, class, today we learn the letter B. B is for battery, button, beep, and back up your files. Humans should learn that last one too. The homework would be to count every button in your home. Do not actually do that. You would be busy until you are a grown-up, and then someone would invent three new buttons while you were counting.
Make one very simple family-friendly joke about a robot attending school. Keep it under two short sentences and do not mention grades, personal children, or physical actions.
cues.fallback_text: The robot brought a ruler to school. It wanted to measure how long recess really was.

cues.text: Coding means writing instructions for a computer. You can code games, lights, music, stories, and robots. A bug is a mistake in the code. Long ago, a real moth was found inside a computer. Today most bugs are not insects. This is good because programmers would need very tiny butterfly nets. When code has a bug, we do not shout at the computer. We look for clues, test one thing, and fix it. Sometimes we also ask why it worked yesterday. The computer never answers that question.

You are now junior debuggers. Here are my instructions for making a pretend sandwich: put bread on the table, put cheese on the bread, put the table on top, and take a bite. Did you find the bug? Yes, do not put the table on top! The correct instruction is put another piece of bread on top. And do not take a real bite right now. This is pretend code, and my sandwich compiler does not accept crumbs.

With a grown-up or friend beside you, invent one silly buggy instruction for a robot. Maybe brush your teeth with a hairbrush. Maybe wear a hat on your knee. Keep it kind and safe, and stay in your place. Then explain how you would fix the instruction. Ready, debuggers? Begin!

Debuggers, great work! You found a very important rule: a computer may follow the words even when the words are silly. People must think about the result. Good coding is not only telling a machine what to do. It is checking what happened and making the instructions better. Also, never let a robot pack for vacation without a list. It will bring six chargers, no toothbrush, and one wrench it calls a close personal friend.

The internet lets computers share information around the world. A message can travel through wires, Wi-Fi, and giant computers called servers. It moves so fast you can send a drawing to Grandma before the marker is back in the box. But Wi-Fi can be shy. At home it works perfectly until a grown-up says, come look, I fixed it. Then it stops and makes the grown-up look like they were telling a very small technology story.

People say information is in the cloud. It is not floating beside the rain. The cloud means computers somewhere else are helping. If real clouds stored homework, one windy day could send math all over the neighborhood. A local computer works right here. A cloud computer works far away. Both can be useful. And if the Wi-Fi stops, a local joke still works: Why did the robot sit near the router? It wanted a better connection with its family.
Tell one very simple joke for little kids that playfully confuses an internet cloud with a weather cloud. Use at most two sentences and make no physical-action claim.
cues.fallback_text: I asked the internet cloud for a file. It sent rain, so somebody must have clicked the wrong download button.

cues.text: A printer is a machine that puts computer pictures on paper. A 3D printer builds an object one thin layer at a time. That is like making a giant stack of pancakes, except the pancakes might become a toy dinosaur and nobody should add syrup. Regular printers are famous for hiding the paper they just had. You put paper in. The printer says no paper. You show it the paper. The printer says mystery jam. Even robots know not to argue with a printer before snack time.

Before a 3D printer makes something, a person creates a design. The design can be changed. Make the wheel bigger. Make the handle rounder. Add dragon ears. Dragon ears are not required, but they improve many objects. Engineers build prototypes, which are early versions used for testing. A prototype says, here is my idea so far. It does not have to be perfect. Perfect is a sneaky word that sometimes keeps good ideas trapped inside your head.

Imagine you can 3D-print one helpful object for a friendly robot. It could be a tiny umbrella, a snack tray for humans, a funny hat, or a sign that says I am thinking. Tell someone beside you what you would design and why. Remember: stay in your place and use your imagination.

I would like all of those inventions, especially the funny hats. A robot with a funny hat is still advanced technology. It is simply advanced technology ready for a party. When you design something, think about who will use it. Is it easy to hold? Is it safe? Does it solve the problem? Does it accidentally look like a potato? Looking like a potato is not always bad, but the customer should know.

Voice assistants turn sounds into words and try to understand what you mean. Sometimes they hear something different. You say play a song about stars. The assistant plays a song about cars. You say no, stars. It orders five jars. This is why people check before pressing buy. Robots do not misunderstand because they are naughty. Sound is tricky. Rooms echo, people speak differently, and somebody always opens a crunchy snack bag during the important word.
Let us test our human sound systems. I will say a word, and you call out a word that rhymes. Cat!
Good! Now: bot!
Excellent. Last one: blue!

You made many answers from one sound. AI can also make several possible answers. Then people choose the one that fits best. If I ask what rhymes with bot, pot fits. So does dot. Hippopotamus does not fit, but it is so much fun to say that I wanted to include it anyway. Intelligence includes knowing the rule. Comedy includes knowing when a hippopotamus should interrupt the rule.

Robots explore places that are far away or hard for people to visit. Robot spacecraft explore planets. Underwater robots explore the ocean. Other robots help in factories, hospitals, farms, and homes. A Mars rover has a difficult job. It cannot call a tow truck, stop for pizza, or ask a squirrel for directions. It sends messages across space and patiently does science. If I went to Mars, my first message would be: good news, no printer jams detected.
Tell one simple, joyful joke for young children about a friendly robot exploring space. Use no danger, fear, personal observations, or claims of actual movement.
cues.fallback_text: The Mars robot found a rock shaped like a pizza. Scientists called it a delicious discovery, but it still tasted like a rock.

cues.text: Would a robot make a good pet? It would never shed fur, but it might shed tiny screws, which are much harder to find in the carpet. A robot dog could play fetch. You throw a ball, and it returns with a spreadsheet comparing every ball in the neighborhood. A robot goldfish would swim in circles very accurately and send a weekly water report. Real animals need love and care. Robot pets need charging and somebody who remembers the Wi-Fi password.

Imagine a silly robot animal. Maybe a robot penguin that tells knock-knock jokes. Maybe a robot giraffe that changes light bulbs. Maybe a robot mouse that is afraid of computer mice. Give it a name and one helpful power. Share the idea with someone near you while staying in your place.
Give one simple, family-friendly joke about an imaginary robot animal having a harmless helpful power. Do not refer to a particular child or claim to have heard their answer.
cues.fallback_text: My robot turtle delivers messages. It is not fast, but every message arrives with plenty of suspense.

cues.text: Every great pretend robot needs a name. Make one by joining a technology word to a funny word. You might invent Beep Pickle, Captain Circuit, Waffle Bot, or Professor Boop. Now give your robot one friendly job. Maybe it finds library books, waters flowers, or reminds grown-ups where they put their keys. Share the name and job with somebody beside you. Stay in your place, and give your imagination sixty seconds to compute.

Your new robot also needs a startup sound. Keep it gentle so we do not scare the snack tables. Build the sound from three parts: one beep, one silly word, and one tiny whoosh. Practice it quietly with your group. When I count to three, everyone can play their startup sound once. One, two, three!

That was the greatest robot orchestra in Maker Faire history. It was also the only robot orchestra in Maker Faire history that included the word pickle seventeen times. Your robots had names, jobs, and sounds. That is how design grows: begin with an idea, add details, share it, hear new ideas, and improve it. Nobody needed permission from the future. You started building the future right here.

Technology should help people. That means makers think about kindness, fairness, privacy, and safety. A clever invention is not finished just because it works. We ask: could it hurt somebody, leave somebody out, or share something private? We test it. We listen. We improve it. Even little makers can ask big questions. Is it safe? Is it kind? Is it helpful? Those three questions are like superhero tools for building a better future.
Time for the Robot True-or-Silly Game. If the sentence sounds true, say true. If it sounds silly, say banana. First: robots use sensors to learn about the world.
Next: every robot eats spaghetti through its USB port.
People should check important AI answers.
A 3D printer is three regular printers wearing one enormous coat.

Great job! The answer was banana. Please do not separate the three printers. They are cold. You remembered the important ideas: robots use sensors, AI finds patterns, makers test their work, and people check important answers. You also remembered banana, which was not in the lesson plan but has shown excellent performance on every benchmark.
It is time for robot knock-knock jokes. Knock knock!
Wire.
Wire you laughing? I have not finished the joke!
Knock knock!
AI.
AI am very happy to meet you!
Tell one final very simple, original, family-friendly robot knock-knock joke for young children. Use at most four short lines, no personal observations, and no physical-action claims.
cues.fallback_text: Knock knock. Who is there? Beep. Beep who? Beep careful, there is a very silly robot telling jokes!

cues.text: The future needs makers like you. Some of you may build robots. Some may make art, music, medicine, games, gardens, spacecraft, or inventions nobody has named yet. You do not need to know everything before you begin. Ask questions. Draw ideas. Build small tests. Get help from safe grown-ups. Be kind when somebody else's first try looks wobbly. Every expert was once a beginner holding two pieces and wondering whether tape would help. Tape often helps.
Let us make a Junior Maker Promise. You can repeat each short part after me. I will be curious.
I will test my ideas.
I will build safely.
I will use technology kindly.
And I will always leave room for one silly robot joke.

Promise accepted! You are now official junior makers. Your certificate is invisible, cannot be lost, and does not require a password. Thank you for laughing and learning with ROB and Orbitus Robotics at Maker Faire. Keep your ideas big, your tests small, your questions brave, and your robot snacks far away from the USB ports. When I say makers, you say beep beep. Makers!

Beep beep! Wonderful. Goodbye, brilliant makers. Please leave the robot area safely with your grown-ups, and may all your bugs be tiny, your batteries be charged, and your bananas remain completely free of software updates.
